```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = NA)
library(mcVarReduce)
```

## 1. Problem

The package studies three variance-reduction methods for the same target,

\[
\theta = \int_0^1 e^x\,dx = e - 1.
\]

Because the exact answer is known, estimation accuracy can be measured directly.

## 2. Control variates

For the main method, `Y = exp(U)` is adjusted with the control variable

\[
C_\alpha = \alpha U + (1-\alpha)V,
\]

where `U` and `V` are independent uniform random variables on `[0, 1]`. The control mean is always 0.5. The value of `alpha` changes how strongly the control is associated with `Y` while the target remains unchanged.

The adjusted contribution is

\[
Z = Y + c(C_\alpha - 0.5).
\]

The coefficient is estimated from an independent pilot sample and is held fixed in the main simulation.

```{r}
strong <- control_variate(
  budget = 5000,
  alpha = 1,
  pilot_fraction = 0.10,
  seed = 8670
)

strong[c(
  "estimate",
  "true_value",
  "correlation",
  "theoretical_correlation",
  "coefficient",
  "theoretical_coefficient",
  "mcse"
)]
```

When `alpha = 1`, a strong positive correlation is expected. A negative control coefficient is expected because the adjustment is written with a plus sign.

A weak-control example can also be run.

```{r}
weak <- control_variate(
  budget = 5000,
  alpha = 0.10,
  pilot_fraction = 0.10,
  seed = 8670
)

weak[c(
  "estimate",
  "true_value",
  "correlation",
  "coefficient",
  "mcse"
)]
```

The weak control is expected to provide much less precision improvement than the strong control.

## 3. Antithetic variables

The antithetic method pairs `U` with `1 - U`. Two target-function evaluations are used for each pair.

```{r}
anti <- antithetic_estimate(
  budget = 5000,
  seed = 8670
)

anti[c(
  "estimate",
  "true_value",
  "pair_correlation",
  "theoretical_pair_correlation",
  "mcse"
)]
```

A negative pair correlation is expected for this monotone target, so the pair average is stabilized.

## 4. Importance sampling

The importance-sampling method uses

\[
q(x) = \frac{2}{3}(1+x), \qquad 0 \le x \le 1.
\]

Samples are generated by inverse transformation and are weighted by `exp(x) / q(x)`.

```{r}
imp <- importance_sampling(
  budget = 5000,
  seed = 8670
)

imp[c("estimate", "true_value", "mcse", "proposal")]
```

The proposal places more probability near larger values of `x`, where `exp(x)` contributes more strongly to the integral.

## 5. Correlation study

The effect of control strength is investigated by changing `alpha` and repeating the control-variate estimator.

```{r}
study <- correlation_study(
  alpha_values = c(0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1),
  budget = 1000,
  replications = 20,
  pilot_fraction = 0.10,
  seed = 8670
)

study$summary
```

The `alpha = 0` setting is a useful limitation case because the control is independent of the target output. A larger budget and more replications can be used for the full experiment.

## 6. Method comparison

The three methods can be compared at the same target-function evaluation budget.

```{r}
comparison <- compare_methods(
  budget = 1000,
  replications = 20,
  alpha = 1,
  pilot_fraction = 0.10,
  seed = 8670
)

comparison$summary
```

RMSE and empirical variance summarize repeated-simulation accuracy. Average MCSE summarizes the uncertainty reported by each estimator, and `mean_time_ms` summarizes computation time. The exact target is used as the accuracy reference.

## 7. Interpretation

The control-variate method is expected to work best when an informative control is available. Antithetic variables depend on a useful negative relationship between paired outputs. Importance sampling depends on a proposal distribution that concentrates sampling effort in useful regions without creating unstable weights. These conditions provide natural limitations to discuss when the three methods are compared.
